q: Who is the author of the lesson "A Baker from Goa"?
e: Lucio Rodrigues wrote "A Baker from Goa"; Lokesh Abrol wrote "Coorg" and Arup Kumar Datta wrote "Tea from Assam".

q: What was the baker from Goa traditionally called? [JAC 2024, 2026]
e: In Goa, the traditional village baker is known as a "pader".

q: How many times did the baker come every day? [JAC 2025]
e: The baker came twice a day—once in the morning on his selling round and again when returning after emptying his basket.

q: The baker’s presence was announced by the sound of his: [JAC 2026]
o: Thud and jingle of his bamboo staff
e: The baker announced his arrival with the "jhang, jhang" thud and jingle of his specially made bamboo staff.

q: Marriage gifts in Goa are meaningless without which sweet bread? [JAC 2020]
e: In Goa, marriage gifts lose their meaning without the sweet bread known as "bol".

q: What must the lady of the house prepare on the occasion of her daughter’s engagement? [JAC 2020]
e: As mentioned in the text, the lady of the house must prepare sandwiches on her daughter’s engagement.

q: Which items are a must for Christmas and other festivals in Goa?
e: Cakes and bolinhas are a must for Christmas as well as other festivals in Goa.

q: What was the baker’s peculiar single-piece long frock reaching down to the knees called?
e: The baker’s peculiar dress was known as "kabai", a single-piece long frock reaching down to the knees.

q: What did the children long for most from the baker’s basket?
e: While elders bought regular loaves, the children eagerly longed for the sweet ring-shaped bread-bangles.

q: Where did the baker in Goa record his monthly accounts?
e: The baker collected his bills at the end of the month, and monthly accounts were written on some wall in pencil.

q: Who is the author of the lesson "Coorg"?
e: Lokesh Abrol is the author of "Coorg".

q: Coorg is situated midway between which two places in Karnataka? [JAC 2026]
o: Mysore and the coastal town of Mangalore
e: Coorg, or Kodagu, Karnataka’s smallest district, lies midway between Mysore and the coastal town of Mangalore.

q: What is the other name of Coorg? [JAC 2025]
e: Coorg is also known as "Kodagu", and its local people are called Kodavus.

q: What percentage of Coorg is covered by evergreen rainforests?
e: According to the chapter, evergreen rainforests cover 30 percent of the Coorg district.

q: When does the "season of joy" (best visiting season) in Coorg occur?
e: In Coorg, the season of joy commences from September and continues till March.

q: Where did General Cariappa, the first Chief of the Indian Army, belong to? [JAC 2023]
e: General Cariappa, the first Chief of the Indian Army, was a Coorgi.

q: Who are the only people in India permitted to carry firearms without a licence? [JAC 2023]
e: Even today, Kodavus are the only people in India permitted to carry firearms without a licence.

q: Which river obtains its water from the hills and forests of Coorg?
e: The River Kaveri obtains its water from the hills and forests of Coorg.

q: What is the name of the large freshwater fish found abundantly in the waters of Coorg?
e: Mahaseer, a large freshwater fish, abounds in the waters of Coorg.

q: Who is the author of "Tea from Assam"?
e: Arup Kumar Datta is the author of "Tea from Assam".

q: Where were Rajvir and Pranjol travelling to by train? [JAC 2026]
e: Pranjol and Rajvir were travelling by train from Delhi to Assam during summer vacation.

q: According to Rajvir, how many cups of tea are drunk every day throughout the world?
e: Rajvir told Pranjol that over eighty crore cups of tea are drunk every day throughout the world.

q: According to the legend shared by Rajvir, where was tea first discovered? [JAC 2026]
e: Tea was first drunk in China as far back as 2700 B.C.; Rajvir shared the legend of a Chinese emperor.

q: When tea came to Europe in the sixteenth century, how was it drunk?
o: More as medicine than as a beverage
e: Tea reached Europe in the sixteenth century and was drunk more as medicine than as a beverage.

q: Which tea-garden was managed by Pranjol’s father?
e: Pranjol’s father was the manager of Dhekiabari, a tea-garden in Upper Assam.

q: Who is the poet of the poem "The Trees"?
e: The poem "The Trees" was written by American feminist poet Adrienne Rich.

q: In the poem "The Trees", where are the trees moving out from?
e: The opening line states that "The trees inside are moving out into the forest."

q: At what time of day do the trees work to disengage themselves in "The Trees"?
e: The poem states that "All night the roots work to disengage themselves from the cracks in the veranda floor."

q: At the end of "The Trees", in the crown of which tree do the pieces of the broken moon flash?
e: In the concluding lines, the pieces of the broken moon flash "in the crown of the tallest oak."

q: In the third stanza of "The Trees", what is the poet doing while sitting inside?
e: Sitting inside with doors open to the veranda, the poet is writing long letters.

q: What was the open testimony to the happy and prosperous life of a Goan baker?
e: Baking was profitable; the baker and his family never starved, and their plump physique was an open testimony to their prosperity.

q: Even today in Goa, a person with a jackfruit-like physical appearance is easily compared to whom?
e: Lucio Rodrigues notes that any person with a jackfruit-like physical appearance is easily compared to a baker.

q: Who invites the comment "He is dressed like a pader!" in Goa? [JAC 2021]
o: Anyone wearing a half-pant reaching just below the knees
Someone wearing a full suit and tie
Someone wearing a long black coat
e: Bakers wore a shirt and trousers shorter than full-length and longer than half-pants; anyone wearing a half-pant reaching just below the knees invites this comment.

q: What did children in Lucio Rodrigues’s childhood eat with hot tea without even brushing their teeth?
e: Children ate bread-bangles with hot tea, reasoning that hot tea washes everything nicely and the tiger never brushed its teeth.

q: What names did Lucio Rodrigues use to refer to the maid-servant of the house who bought the loaves?
e: The author mentions that the loaves for the family were bought by some "Paskine or Bastine, the maid-servant of the house."

q: When greeting the lady of the house, where did the baker place his basket?
e: After greeting the lady with "Good morning," the baker placed his basket on the vertical bamboo.

q: What historical theory supports the Greek descent of the people of Coorg?
o: A part of Alexander’s army moved south along the coast and settled there when return became impractical
Greek kings ruled Karnataka for a century
Greek merchants came by sea to sell coffee
e: One story says a part of Alexander’s army moved south along the coast, settled in Coorg when return became impractical, and married amongst the locals.

q: The "kuppia" worn by the Kodavus resembles the traditional dress of which groups?
o: The "kuffia" worn by Arabs and Kurds
e: The long, black coat with an embroidered waist-belt known as kuppia resembles the kuffia worn by Arabs and Kurds.

q: Climbing which hills brings one to a panoramic view of the entire misty landscape of Coorg?
e: The climb to the Brahmagiri hills brings you into a panoramic view of the entire misty landscape of Coorg.

q: Walking across the rope bridge in Coorg leads to which sixty-four-acre island?
e: A walk across the rope bridge leads to the sixty-four-acre island of Nisargadhama.

q: Nearby Bylakuppe in Coorg is famous for housing India’s largest settlement of which community?
e: Bylakuppe near Coorg is India’s largest Tibetan settlement, where visitors encounter Buddhist monks in red, ochre, and yellow robes.

q: Which high-energy adventure sports are available in Coorg?
o: River rafting, canoeing, rappelling, rock climbing, and mountain biking
e: Coorg offers high-energy adventures including river rafting, canoeing, rappelling, rock climbing, and mountain biking.

q: Why do squirrels and langurs drop partially eaten fruit into the clear water of Coorg?
o: For the mischief of enjoying the splash and the ripple effect in clear water
e: Squirrels and langurs drop partially eaten fruit for the mischief of enjoying the splash and the ripple effect in the clear water.

q: Which animals keep a watchful eye from the tree canopy in Coorg?
o: Macaques, Malabar squirrels, langurs, and slender loris
e: Macaques, Malabar squirrels, langurs, and slender loris keep a watchful eye from the tree canopy.

q: Why did Pranjol NOT share Rajvir’s excitement at seeing the tea garden from the train?
o: Pranjol had been born and brought up on a plantation
e: Pranjol had been born and brought up on a tea plantation, so he didn’t share Rajvir’s excitement and kept reading his detective book.

q: How did Rajvir describe the tea-pluckers moving amidst the orderly rows of tea bushes from the train?
e: From a distance, amidst the orderly rows of tea bushes, the tea-pluckers appeared to Rajvir as busily moving "doll-like figures".

q: According to the Indian legend in "Tea from Assam", which Buddhist ascetic cut off his eyelids?
e: Bodhidharma, an ancient Buddhist ascetic, cut off his eyelids because he felt sleepy during meditations; ten tea plants grew out of them.

q: According to the Indian legend, how many tea plants grew out of Bodhidharma’s eyelids?
e: Ten tea plants grew out of the eyelids, and their leaves put in hot water and drunk banished sleep.

q: Words such as "tea", "chai", and "chini" originate from which language?
e: Rajvir notes that words like "tea", "chai", and "chini" are from Chinese.

q: At which railway junction did Rajvir and Pranjol get down in Assam?
e: The train clattered into Mariani junction, where Pranjol’s parents were waiting to receive them.

q: After crossing a cattle-bridge, Pranjol’s father’s car entered which estate?
e: They crossed a cattle-bridge and entered Dhekiabari Tea Estate along a gravel-road.

q: Which months mark the "second-flush" or sprouting period that yields the best tea?
e: The second-flush or sprouting period lasts from May to July and yields the best quality tea.

q: What were the tea-pluckers at Dhekiabari wearing as they plucked newly sprouted leaves?
o: Bamboo baskets on their backs and plastic aprons
e: Groups of tea-pluckers had bamboo baskets on their backs and wore plastic aprons while plucking newly sprouted leaves.

q: According to "The Trees", what could NOT happen in the empty forest?
o: No bird could sit, no insect hide, and no sun bury its feet in shadow
e: In the treeless forest, no bird could sit, no insect could hide, and no sun could bury its feet in shadow.

q: What does the poet compare the long-cramped boughs of the trees to in "The Trees"? [JAC 2019]
o: Newly discharged patients half-dazed moving to the clinic doors
e: The long-cramped boughs shuffling under the roof are compared to newly discharged patients, half-dazed, moving to the clinic doors.

q: What does the poet "scarcely mention" in her long letters?
o: The departure of the forest from the house
e: The poet writes long letters "in which I scarcely mention the departure of the forest from the house."

q: In "The Trees", how does the smell of leaves and lichen reach into the rooms?
e: The poem says the smell of leaves and lichen "still reaches like a voice into the rooms", evoking sensory longing.

q: In the final stanza of "The Trees", what rushes forward to meet the stumbling trees?
e: As the glass breaks and the trees stumble forward into the night, "Winds rush to meet them."

q: What fills the poet’s head tonight that "tomorrow will be silent" in "The Trees"?
e: The poet says her head is "full of whispers which tomorrow will be silent" once the trees have departed into the forest.

q: How did the tea vendor cry out on the train at the start of "Tea from Assam"?
e: The narrative opens with a high-pitched vendor calling out "Chai-garam... garam-chai!"

q: "Those eaters of loaves might have vanished, but the makers are still there." What does this line signify?
o: All bakeries in Goa are permanently shut
Only rice is eaten in Goa now
Portuguese rulers left, yet the traditional art and furnaces of baking still survive in Goa
e: Though the old Portuguese patrons have passed on, their descendants continue the baking craft with the same age-old furnaces.

q: In "A Baker from Goa", what does "The fire in the furnaces has not yet been extinguished" symbolically mean?
o: Fire hazards remain common in Goa
The age-old Portuguese baking tradition is still alive and thriving
Bakers forget to turn off ovens
e: Figuratively, it means the traditional Goan profession and cultural legacy of baking continue uninterrupted into the present.

q: In "We kids would be pushed aside with a mild rebuke", what does "rebuke" mean?
o: A mild scolding or expression of disapproval
e: "Rebuke" means a sharp disapproval or scolding; the baker gently scolded and pushed the eager children aside.

q: In "their plump physique was an open testimony to this", what does "testimony" mean in context?
e: Here "testimony" means clear evidence or proof—their plump bodies publicly proved that baking was a prosperous trade.

q: Based on "A Baker from Goa", if a village baker’s furnace closed permanently, which cultural occasions would immediately lose their essential traditions?
o: Marriage gifts, a daughter’s engagement, and Christmas festivals
e: Without the baker, weddings would lack bol, engagements would lack sandwiches, and Christmas would miss cakes and bolinhas.

q: "...a piece of heaven that must have drifted from the kingdom of god." What does the phrase "drifted from" suggest here?
o: Carried gently or floated down from heaven onto Earth
e: It conveys the poetic imagery of Coorg being so heavenly that it seems to have floated gently down from God’s kingdom.

q: In the Coorg extract, "proud race of martial men", what does the word "martial" mean? [JAC 2019]
o: Having to do with war and bravery
e: "Martial" means relating to war, fighting, or military valour—reflecting the Kodavus’ proud warrior heritage.

q: In "The air breathes invigorating coffee", what does "invigorating" mean?
e: "Invigorating" means making one feel healthy, fresh, and full of energy.

q: Why does Coorg receive very few visitors during the monsoon season according to the text?
o: It pours heavily enough to keep many visitors away
e: The text explicitly states that during the monsoons, "it pours enough to keep many visitors away."

q: What sequence of experiences would a trekker visiting Brahmagiri hills, Nisargadhama, and Bylakuppe encounter?
o: Misty panoramic hills, a 64-acre island via a rope bridge, and Tibetan Buddhist monks
e: Together they showcase misty hill panoramas, the 64-acre island across a rope bridge, and the Tibetan settlement’s Buddhist culture.

q: What does "Elephants enjoy being bathed and scrubbed in the river by their mahouts" illustrate about Coorg?
o: Harmonious coexistence between humans and nature/wildlife
e: It reflects the joyful and harmonious bond between local people, wildlife, and the river environment of Coorg.

q: "Dwarfing the tiny tea plants were tall sturdy shade-trees." What practical purpose do these tall shade-trees serve in tea estates?
o: They are planted solely for timber export
They shield delicate tea bushes from harsh direct sunlight and preserve moisture
They dry out the tea bushes
e: Tall shade-trees protect tender tea plants from scorching sunlight while maintaining a humid microclimate ideal for leaf growth.

q: Why did Pranjol’s father remark to Rajvir, "You seem to have done your homework before coming"?
o: Because Rajvir accurately knew about the May–July second-flush sprouting period producing the best tea
Because Rajvir had worked as a plucker before
Because Rajvir lived next door in Assam
Because Rajvir finished his maths notebook on the train
e: Rajvir impressed Pranjol’s father by knowing that the May–July second-flush period yields the finest tea.

q: Although Rajvir was an ardent fan of detective stories, why did he skip reading on the train to Assam?
o: He had lost his detective novel
The lush green scenery and endless tea gardens outside fascinated him far more
There were no lights inside the coach
e: Visiting Assam for the first time, Rajvir was captivated by the green paddy fields giving way to vast stretches of tea bushes.

q: Which poetic device is used in the line "no sun bury its feet in shadow" in "The Trees"?
e: The sun is given human attributes ("feet" that can be buried in shadow), making it a clear example of personification.

q: Identify the figure of speech in "The moon is broken like a mirror" from "The Trees":
e: The explicit comparison using "like" between the moon (fragmented by tree branches) and a broken mirror is a Simile.

q: Why does the full moon suddenly appear "broken like a mirror" at the end of "The Trees"?
o: Because the branches and crown of the tall oak tree now stood in front of the moon, fragmenting its view
Because broken glass hit the moon
Because heavy storm clouds covered the sky
e: Earlier the whole moon shone in an open sky, but once the tall oak moved outside, its dense branches visually fractured the moon into flashing pieces.

q: Which poetic device is highlighted in the phrases "long letters" and "leaves and lichen" in "The Trees"?
e: Repetition of the initial consonant sound /l/ in closely placed words ("long letters", "leaves and lichen") is Alliteration.

q: What does "Listen. The glass is breaking." indicate literally and figuratively in "The Trees"?
o: The poet angrily smashed the mirror
A kitchen dish fell on the floor
The straining trees shatter the confining glass barrier as they break free into the night
A sudden hailstorm shattered the roof
e: Literally, straining leaves and twigs push through and break the glass pane; symbolically, it marks the shattering of domestic confinement.

q: What does "small twigs stiff with exertion" convey about the trees’ escape in "The Trees"?
o: Winter frost has frozen the twigs
The trees are afraid to leave the house
The trees have already withered and died
Breaking free from confinement demands immense, exhausting effort
e: It emphasizes the strenuous, persistent struggle required by every part of the tree to liberate itself from unnatural confinement.

q: Identify the poetic device in "the smell of leaves and lichen / still reaches like a voice into the rooms":
e: It uses a Simile ("like a voice") while blending olfactory (smell) and auditory (voice) imagery.

q: In "A Baker from Goa", what did the children do after being pushed aside so they could still see the bread-bangles?
o: Climbed a bench or the parapet and peeped into the basket
e: Refusing to give up, the children climbed onto a bench or the parapet to peep into the basket and pick bread-bangles.

q: Why did Pranjol’s father slow down on the gravel-road inside Dhekiabari Tea Estate?

The car was running out of fuel
To allow a tractor pulling a trailer-load of tea leaves to pass
To let Rajvir pluck a tea bud
e: He slowed down on the narrow gravel-road so a tractor pulling a trailer-load of tea leaves could pass safely.

Rajvir was thrilled seeing tea gardens for the first time, whereas Pranjol grew up amidst them and remained calm
Pranjol cried seeing the fields while Rajvir slept
e: Familiarity dulled Pranjol’s wonder since he grew up on a plantation, whereas Rajvir experienced fresh amazement.

q: What is the rhyme scheme of Adrienne Rich’s poem "The Trees"?
e: Adrienne Rich composed "The Trees" in free verse with no regular rhyme scheme or rigid metre.

q: In "Coorg", what does "the most laidback individuals become converts to the life of high-energy adventure" mean?
o: Even the most relaxed people get inspired to try thrilling adventure sports in Coorg
Locals in Coorg refuse to work
Adventure sports are banned for tourists
e: The natural beauty and adventure opportunities of Coorg inspire even relaxed, easy-going visitors to take up exciting activities.

q: Why are the trees described as "stumbling forward into the night" in the final stanza of "The Trees"?

Because the night is freezing cold
Because having been cramped indoors for so long, they move clumsily like recovering patients stepping into freedom
Because they wish to re-enter the house
e: Having remained cramped under the roof for so long, they step awkwardly yet eagerly into freedom, extending the earlier patient simile.

q: In "Tea from Assam", what was the "ugly building with smoke billowing out of tall chimneys" spotted near the sea of tea bushes?
e: The smoking building rising amid the sea of tea bushes was a tea factory processing the plucked leaves.

q: What does "The thud and jingle of the traditional baker’s bamboo can still be heard in some places" reveal about contemporary Goa?

e: The author humorously notes that while smaller creatures watch from the canopy, he himself prefers to step aside for wild elephants.

q: By noting that "the mixers, the moulders and the furnaces" still survive in Goa, what broader insight does Lucio Rodrigues convey?

e: Despite political transitions, the continuation of baking by the paders’ sons highlights resilient cultural continuity.

q: In "The Trees", why does the poet sit inside "writing long letters / in which I scarcely mention the departure of the forest"?

The poet ran out of ink and paper
The exodus of trees was trivial and unnoticed
The poet hated trees and wanted them gone
e: Her silence highlights human detachment or reluctance to acknowledge major ecological and social revolutions occurring right before their eyes.

q: What fundamental conflict does "The Trees" explore through the movement of trees from inside a house to the forest?
o: A debate between poets and painters
The conflict between artificial human confinement (control) and nature’s innate urge for freedom
A trade dispute between cities and villages
A seasonal clash between winter and summer
e: It dramatizes the tension between humanity’s desire to tame/confine nature (or women) and their irrepressible drive toward authentic freedom.

q: In "The Trees", what do the "whispers" filling the poet’s head most deeply symbolise?
o: The restless murmurs of trapped trees (and suppressed voices) striving to break free before departing into peace
Static noise from an indoor radio
e: They represent the urgent, quiet stirrings of trapped beings preparing to break free—silenced once liberation is achieved by dawn.

q: How does the story of Coorg’s Greek/Arab cultural roots combined with General Cariappa’s leadership enrich the theme of "Glimpses of India"?

e: Embracing possible Greek or Arab cultural influences while producing India’s first Army Chief exemplifies unity in diversity.

q: Why did Arup Kumar Datta include both a Chinese legend and an Indian legend about the origin of tea in "Tea from Assam"?

Because Rajvir wanted to confuse his friend
Because legends help tea leaves grow faster
e: Pairing the accidental Chinese discovery with Bodhidharma’s meditative discipline illustrates how tea spans culinary delight and spiritual tradition across Asia.

q: In "The Trees", how does the shift from "the whole moon shines in a sky still open" to "The moon is broken like a mirror" function symbolically?
o: It signals an approaching dust storm
The fractured moon crowns the liberated oak tree, symbolising broken old norms and nature’s triumphant renewal
It predicts the literal destruction of Earth
e: Far from defeat, the shattered moon flashes like a royal crown atop the tallest oak, celebrating the trees’ victorious reclamation of the wild.

e: Lucio Rodrigues uses this charming childhood rationalisation to give the memoir warmth, humour, and vivid nostalgia.

q: What does the children’s refusal to give up despite a "mild rebuke" reveal about the baker’s role in the village?

The baker gave away every loaf free of cost
Children merely plotted to topple his basket
Children feared the baker and hid inside
e: Even his mild rebuke was playful; the pader served as friend, companion, and guide whose daily visits thrilled the children.

q: How do Coorg’s geography and climate (rolling hills, 30% rainforests, Kaveri, coffee) shape its human and ecological identity?

They turn Coorg into a barren desert
They force every inhabitant to migrate to cities
e: Its hilly isolation and lush forests nurtured the Kodavus’ fiercely independent character, rich wildlife, coffee estates, and adventure culture.

q: What contrast in attitudes does Arup Kumar Datta draw between Pranjol burying his nose in a detective book and Rajvir gazing out the window?

A lazy student vs. a strict teacher
e: It highlights how familiarity often breeds indifference in locals, while an outsider’s fresh curiosity uncovers wonder and knowledge.

q: In a metaphorical reading of "The Trees", what do the "cracks in the veranda floor" and "the roof" represent?
o: Social, domestic, and patriarchal constraints through which the trapped struggle to force an exit to freedom
e: The veranda floor and low roof symbolise restrictive domestic and societal boundaries, while the cracks signify fragile openings toward freedom.

q: Why did the narrator call the baker "our friend, companion and guide" in "A Baker from Goa"?
o: Because he taught English at the village school
Because he served as the village magistrate
Because his regular twice-daily visits, playful interactions, and sweet bread-bangles anchored their daily childhood routine
e: His dependable twice-daily rounds, gentle teasing, and special treats made him an intimate anchor in the children’s daily lives.

q: What narrative purpose does mentioning the rope bridge to Nisargadhama and Buddhist monks at Bylakuppe serve at the end of "Coorg"?

It claims concrete bridges cannot exist there
It warns tourists against entering the island
e: It rounds out the essay by adding spiritual serenity as a bonus to wild adventure before calling Coorg "the heart and soul of India."

q: Why does Adrienne Rich contrast "the forest that was empty all these days" with "empty all these nights" in Stanza 1 of "The Trees"?

Because she forgot the difference between day and night
To maintain a strict AABB rhyme scheme
e: Repeating the emptiness across both "days" and "nights" intensifies the unnatural, continuous desolation of a treeless forest.

q: In light of "A Baker from Goa", what would be lost if traditional village bakers were entirely replaced by automated supermarket factories?
o: Personal community bonds, festive ritual craftsmanship (bol, bolinhas), and the living heritage of the village pader
e: Factory bread cannot replace the personal warmth, festive heritage, and community presence embodied by the traditional Goan pader.

e: Despite his impressive preparation, Rajvir stays humble and eager to deepen his knowledge through direct observation on the estate.

q: What natural plant phenomenon parallels "The leaves strain toward the glass" in Adrienne Rich’s "The Trees"?
o: Phototropism—plants instinctively growing and straining toward light and open air
e: Plants naturally reach toward sunlight and open space (phototropism), which the poet elevates into a metaphor for irrepressible liberation.

q: What does pairing General Cariappa’s legacy with Kodavus’ unique firearm privilege tell the reader about Indian state trust in Coorg?
o: It means carrying guns is compulsory for tourists
It reflects extraordinary national trust in the Kodavus’ martial discipline, loyalty, and valour
It implies state laws do not apply in Karnataka
It suggests no police force exists in Coorg
e: The Kodavus’ distinguished military service and disciplined martial code earned them this rare, enduring legal privilege.

q: Why does Adrienne Rich shift to a direct imperative "Listen. The glass is breaking." in the last stanza of "The Trees"?
o: To stop someone from reading her letter
To frighten the trees into stopping
To draw the reader in as an active witness to the decisive moment when quiet endurance finally shatters confinement
Because a burglar broke into the house
e: The sudden imperative pulls the reader from passive observation into witnessing the dramatic climax where silent struggle breaks barriers.

q: What does the scene of maids buying loaves while children eagerly chase bread-bangles reveal about social life in old Goan villages?

The baker only spoke to wealthy landlords

e: Monthly pencil accounts on walls and playful morning exchanges paint a warm picture of close-knit community trust.

q: Why does Lokesh Abrol blend factual details (30% rainforest, September–March) with lyrical phrases ("drifted from the kingdom of god") in "Coorg"?

e: Combining concrete facts with evocative imagery makes "Coorg" both informative as a travelogue and emotionally captivating.

q: How does tea function as a unifying cultural motif connecting Delhi and Upper Assam in "Tea from Assam"?

Delhi has the world’s largest tea estates
e: From the crowded Delhi-to-Assam train compartment to global daily consumption, tea acts as a living bridge between local labour and universal culture.

q: In "The Trees", how will "tomorrow" be different inside the poet’s house after the trees’ departure?

e: Tomorrow brings peace/silence inside the empty room and vibrant ecological renewal outside in the restored forest.

q: Looking closely at the imagery of the broken glass and broken moon at the end of "The Trees", what nuance does it add to the theme of freedom?

Nature should remain permanently potted indoors

e: The shattering glass and fragmented moon suggest that liberation disrupts tidy illusions and old barriers before crowning the freed spirit.

q: The chapter opens with elders "reminiscently/nostalgically" recalling "those good old Portuguese days." How does this opening shape the reader’s lens?

It demands the return of Portuguese colonial rule
It mocks the elders of Goa
It turns the essay into a horror story
e: It frames the essay with warm fondness for memory while proving that cultural craft endures beyond colonial eras.

q: If a cultural historian investigates the origins of the Kodavus using evidence from "Coorg", which two primary clues exist in the chapter?
o: Distinct martial/marriage/religious rites (Greek theory) and the embroidered waist-belt coat "kuppia" matching the Arab "kuffia" (Arab theory)
Old tea and coffee purchase bills
e: Abrol cites distinct martial/religious customs (linking to Alexander’s army) and the kuppia-kuffia garment similarity as historical clues.

He wanted to send Rajvir back to Delhi immediately
He is seasoned, gracious, and appreciative of genuine curiosity in young learners

e: Though an experienced estate manager, he warmly applauds the young visitor’s preparation, creating an encouraging close to the lesson.

q: Across all three prose parts of "Glimpses of India" and the poem "The Trees", how do tradition and nature interact?
o: All four pieces praise polluted industrial megacities
All four advocate cutting down rainforests
All four pieces take place inside one Goan bakery

e: While the prose pieces celebrate regional culture rooted in land and craft, Rich’s poem reminds us that nature belongs wild and unconfined.

q: What subtle change between past and present does Lucio Rodrigues note regarding bakers’ attire and earnings in "A Baker from Goa"?

Cakes are no longer baked for Christmas in Goa
e: While clothing evolved from the kabai to knee-length trousers, the baker’s community role, sound, and prosperous reputation remained recognisable.
